newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Merrill Lynch suit against Singapore banker sealed.
newsitem.headline: Merrill Lynch suit against Singapore banker sealed.

text.p: A lawsuit filed in the Singapore High Court by U.S. merchant bank Merrill Lynch and Co Inc against an ex-employee on suspicion of fraud has been sealed to protect confidential customer accounts, a court official said on Monday.
Officials at the High Court told Reuters an application made last week for the release of details concerning Merrill Lynch's case against Kevin James Wallace had been rejected.
Wallace was a former private client financial consultant with Merrill Lynch.
"The court has ordered that the file can only be inspected with the leave of the court in view of the confidentiality of customer accounts," one official told Reuters.
He said that normally most court files could be inspected, but in this case permission had to be sought from the judge.
Requests had been made by parties involved to keep the case off limits due to the confidentiality of accounts, he said.
A Merrill Lynch spokesman told Reuters from Hong Kong on Friday the company had started civil proceedings in Singapore and Hong Kong against Wallace, who was fired last month.
The spokesman was unable to comment on the amount in question but industry sources and media reports have estimated that some US$30 million could be involved.
Merrill Lynch in Singapore on Monday referred all queries to its Hong Kong spokesman, who was not available for comment.
The whereabouts of Wallace were not known.
In its statement of claim, the company said the former employee had "engaged in unauthorised trading, misrepresenting or falsifying private clients' statements and forging client signatures".

The spokesman said last week that Merrill Lynch had filed a criminal complaint in Singapore and was working closely with the relevant regulatory authorities. Merrill Lynch has sought to freeze Wallace's assets internationally and prevent their dissipation.
Wallace was "let go from Merrill Lynch effective May 15, 1997," the spokesman said.
"Subsequent to his departure from Merrill Lynch it had become apparent Mr Wallace had engaged in inappropriate conduct in some private client accounts," he added.
Officials of Singapore's de-facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and its white-collar crime bureau, the Commercial Affairs Department, declined comment on the case.
An industry source described Wallace as "one of the top brokers within Merrill handling huge accounts".
Local media reported an internal Merrill Lynch inquiry was expected to flesh out details of the alleged crime.
